entry.evidence: In this study, we introduce a fully coupled ice-sheet–climate model as a tool for paleo-climate research.

sequences.source_document: Publisher XML full text (jats_text) with the published PDF

steps.action: Take from published proxy work that sea level and temperature oscillated with a roughly 100 kyr timescale over the last million years.
steps.quote: Geological proxy data show that sea level and surface temperature significantly oscillated with a preferred timescale of about 100 kyr

steps.action: Identify the gap: no global, million-year, coupled ice-sheet– [...] exist.
steps.quote: as far as we know, there are currently no global, million-year, coupled ice-sheet– [...] .

steps.action: Use the authors' existing GREB energy balance climate model, with its flux corrections and hydrological cycle, as the base.
steps.quote: The GREB model is developed and fully described in Dommenget and Flöter (2011)

steps.action: Build a global thermomechanical ice sheet model (4-layer terrain-following grid, SIA for grounded ice, SSA for shelves, surface mass balance, calving, ice energy balance) on the GREB grid.
steps.quote: The ice sheet model is a global thermomechanical ice flow model that comprises momentum balance, mass balance and energy balance modules

steps.action: Compare the simulated seasonal cycle of land snow cover and sea ice extent with observations.
steps.quote: The overall snow cover (land) distribution and seasonal cycle resemble observations (Robinson et al., 2012).

steps.action: Couple the ice sheet to GREB: ice latent heat flux, land precipitation flux correction on zonal-mean humidity, prognostic sea ice, ice-thickness albedo, variable topography, lapse-rate sensible heat, sea level and land–sea mask.
steps.quote: The introduction of an ice sheet model requires a number of changes to the original GREB model.

steps.action: Run short response experiments (10 m ice cover over Europe; 1000 m topography lift) against control runs to check the coupled terms behave as intended.
steps.quote: a simple response experiment in which we add a 10 m ice cover and evaluate how surface temperature responds to it

steps.action: Revise the atmospheric diffusion coefficient upward by a factor of 5 because the earlier GREB had too weak meridional heat transport.
steps.quote: we enhance this diffusion coefficient by a factor of 5

steps.action: Choose the EISMINT I and II community benchmark experiments to test the stand-alone ice sheet model.
steps.quote: use standard experiments from the European Ice Sheet Modelling Initiative (EISMINT) model intercomparison

steps.action: Compare EISMINT I fixed- and moving-margin steady state and oscillating-forcing results with the H96 model ensemble.
steps.quote: The GREB-ISM simulations of the ice thickness at divide and mass flux at midpoint are mostly similar to those found in H96

steps.action: Rerun the mismatched cases in Cartesian coordinates and with 10 vertical layers; the mass flux and basal temperature mismatches disappear (not shown).
steps.quote: This mismatch disappears if we increase the vertical resolution to 10 layers (not shown).

steps.action: Compare EISMINT II experiments A, B and C with the P2000 ensemble; most quantities lie in range, basal melt fraction is biased by a cold bed.
steps.quote: are all within the range of the models in P2000, indicating a fairly good agreement

steps.action: Keep the ice sheet dynamics as fit for global simulations despite the basal temperature bias.
steps.quote: which suggests the model is appropriate for global climate and ice evolution simulations

steps.action: Run a 200 kyr stand-alone global equilibrium forced by present-day climatology and compare ice volume, calving and thickness with observations; West Antarctica gains too much ice.
steps.quote: The West Antarctic ice sheet thickness increase is inconsistent with the observed values, suggesting a model limitation.

steps.action: Vary precipitation forcing, shelf viscosity, sliding coefficient (6e3 to 6e5 per yr) and a basal melting scheme to remove the West Antarctic bias; none removes it.
steps.quote: [...] find the specific limitation that is causing West Antarctic Ice Sheet bias.

steps.action: Compare simulated surface velocities with MEaSUREs observations for Antarctica and Greenland.
steps.quote: Greenland ice velocities are also in good agreement with observations

steps.action: Design a 250 kyr transient experiment scaling present-day to LGM (AWI-ESM) temperature and precipitation patterns by the GRIP δ18O record.
steps.quote: We therefore design an experiment, in which we force the GREB-ISM with surface temperature and precipitation over the past 250 kyr

steps.action: Compare simulated sea level with the marine δ18O proxy (r = −0.67) and observed 120 m range, LGM ice sheets with prior studies, and ice volumes with Fyke et al. (2011).
steps.quote: The two curves show similar time series variations with a correlation of - 0.67.

steps.action: Keep that the stand-alone ice sheet responds realistically to time-varying forcing; attribute the Antarctic difference from Fyke et al. to setup.
steps.quote: the GREB-ISM ice sheet model does have realistic responses to time-varying boundary conditions

steps.action: Run the fully coupled 200 kyr present-day equilibrium and compare surface temperature, precipitation, ice volume and thickness with observations and with the stand-alone run.
steps.quote: the coupled GREB-ISM system converges towards an equilibrium state close to the observed one

steps.action: Design idealized Northern Hemisphere shortwave oscillation runs with 20, 50 and 100 kyr periods.
steps.quote: The oscillation period, pd, is set to 20, 50 and 100 kyr in three individual simulations.

steps.action: Observe that oscillating forcing with unchanged mean produces a mean Northern Hemisphere cooling and larger mean ice volume.
steps.quote: This suggests that the oscillating shortwave radiation has a mean cooling effect.

steps.action: Propose, without testing, that the mean cooling arises from the asymmetric ice–albedo response.
steps.quote: It is beyond this study to fully explore how this effect arises, but it is likely to be related to the ice–albedo effect.

steps.action: Describe slow buildup and fast decay, phase lags, hemispheric teleconnection, larger response at longer periods, and infer NH ice sheet timescales exceed 100 kyr.
steps.quote: the ice sheet growth and decay is asymmetric, with a slower buildup and faster decay in ice volume

steps.action: Suggest, without testing, that coarse resolution of West Antarctic topography causes the residual ice sheet bias.
steps.quote: So, the coarse grid resolution of this model is likely to play a role in this limitation (Cuzzone et al., 2019).

steps.action: Keep GREB-ISM as a fast, fully coupled global ice sheet–climate model suited to 100 kyr and longer simulations.
steps.quote: we presented a new model that is suited for the simulations of global-scale climate variability on timescales of 100 kyr and longer

tree.answer: Quaternary ice-age cycles of about 100 kyr, known from proxies
No; ice–climate interactions over 100 kyr need coupled simulation
Build and characterize a coupled global ice sheet–climate model
None; benchmarks and observations serve as references
Conditions set in model experiments (EISMINT, present-day, δ18O-scaled, idealized insolation)
Partly: benchmarks and observations agree except West Antarctic bias and cold basal temperature
Model kept as suited for 100 kyr+ global simulations
Reviewed by two referees; no review file supplied

end.claim: GREB-ISM is a fully coupled global ice sheet–climate model that matches EISMINT benchmarks and present-day ice sheets (except a West Antarctic excess), and runs about 100 kyr per day on a desktop.

decisive_move.sentence: Building the ice sheet model and coupling it to GREB (precipitation correction, sea ice, albedo, topography, sea level) creates the capability the whole claim characterizes.

gates.evidence: No hypothesis directed data acquisition; experiments chosen to evaluate a new model. Benchmarks could fail and partly did (West Antarctic excess, basal melt fraction, §4.3 ¶3, §4.2 ¶1), but no pass criteria were stated. The EISMINT protocols (H96, P2000) were fixed in advance by the community, but no thresholds or analyses were registered; ηSSA was tuned to observations used in the evaluation (§3.2.4 ¶5).

imports.item: Gauss–Jacobi quadrature with 2-point Gaussian nodes and cubic polynomial fit for vertical integration (Hildebrand, 1987)

novelty_claims.quote: as far as we know, there are currently no global, million-year, coupled ice-sheet– [...] .
We introduce a newly developed global ice sheet model coupled to the Globally Resolved Energy Balance (GREB) climate model
Most previous studies only simulate Northern or Southern Hemisphere ice sheets and take the others as prescribed boundary conditions

limits:
Sub-claims at other statuses:
- EISMINT agreement: capability_characterized, with a cold basal bias.
- Realistic transient response for Greenland and Northern Hemisphere ice sheets: capability_characterized; Antarctica is 'less conclusive' (§6 ¶4).
- Oscillation-experiment findings (mean cooling, slow buildup and fast decay, NH ice sheet timescale >100 kyr): model-internal regularities with no observational test, at most regularity_in_range within the model.
- Ice–albedo explanation of the cooling (§5.2 ¶3) and coarse-resolution explanation of the West Antarctic bias (§6 ¶3): untested hypotheses, status none.

Process the document does not show:
- Several checks are reported as 'not shown': the Cartesian EISMINT I rerun, the 10-layer run, and the LGM forcing pattern.
- The West Antarctic sensitivity tests are described only qualitatively.
- Inference: ηSSA was set to match observed velocity and calving in the same stand-alone equilibrium experiment later used for evaluation (§3.2.4 ¶5). Flux corrections tie temperature and land precipitation to observations (§6 ¶5). Agreement with present-day observations is therefore partly by construction.
- A supplement exists but was not supplied.
- Two referees are acknowledged, but no review file or discussion was supplied, so there is no review sequence.

Locator note: the XML text gives both 'Calving' and 'Momentum balance' the locator §3.2.4. The viscosity steps cite the Momentum balance paragraphs; quotes disambiguate.

disagreements.target: Bueler and Brown (2009) and other ice shelf models
disagreements.support: The paper uses a much higher constant shelf viscosity, tuned to observed shelf thickness, and notes this may absorb basal melting and other uncertainties.
disagreements.quote: The viscosity ( η SSA ) in our model is larger than in other models (Bueler and Brown, 2009).

disagreements.target: EISMINT I model ensemble (Huybrechts et al., 1996, H96)
disagreements.support: Moving-margin mass flux is larger and divide basal temperature 1–2 °C colder; attributed to mesh shape and vertical resolution by unshown reruns.
disagreements.quote: The ice mass flux in the GREB-ISM is larger than in H96 for the moving margin experiment.

disagreements.target: EISMINT II model ensemble (Payne et al., 2000, P2000)
disagreements.support: Basal melt fraction is underestimated by about 30% and its changes in experiments B and C deviate; attributed to a cold bed bias.
disagreements.quote: [...] fraction is underestimated by the GREB-ISM by about 30 %, which is related to a cold bias at the bed of the [...]

disagreements.target: Fyke et al. (2011) LIG, LGM and Late Holocene ice volumes
disagreements.support: Greenland is similar but more variable; Antarctica shows almost no variation, attributed to differing ice shelf parameterization setups (Table 7).
disagreements.quote: The difference between the GREB-ISM model and Fyke et al. (2011) in Antarctica ice sheet may be due to different experimental setups.

disagreements.target: Original GREB diffusion coefficient (Dommenget and Flöter, 2011; Dommenget et al., 2019)
disagreements.support: The value is called weakly constrained; raising it fivefold reduces high-latitude and tropical temperature biases without raising biases elsewhere.
disagreements.quote: This value is not strongly constrained by observations and may effectively be different by an order of magnitude.
